Gamma-Ray Spectra
Shah Kunj Dhirubhai Ambani University (Formerly DAIICT)
Gandhinagar, Gujarat, India
Student ID: 202511031 Program: M.Tech (ICT) Prof. Bhaskar Chaudhary (Supervisor)
Dr. Shishir Purohit (Supervisor)

Abstract —Gamma-ray spectroscopy is widely used in nuclear physics, radiation safety, and environmental monitoring to identify radioactive isotopes based on their characteristic energy peaks. However, in real-world conditions, spectra often contain signals from multiple isotopes at the same time, leading to overlapping peaks that make automatic identification difficult.In this work, we present a seven-step automated pipeline for analyzing mixed gamma-ray spectra. The proposed method includes background removal using the SNIP algorithm, peak detection using Savitzky–Golay smoothing and threshold-based methods, overlap detection using AIC/BIC model selection, and multi-Gaussian fitting to separate overlapping peaks. Finally, isotopes are identified by matching peak positions and areas with a reference energy database.The system was tested on mixed spectra containing five isotopes (Ba-133, Eu-152, Cs-137, Na-22, and Co-60). The results show a precision of 1.000, recall of 0.806, and F1-score of 0.892, indicating accurate identification with very few false positives.These results demonstrate that the proposed pipeline is effective for handling complex spectra and can be further improved by incorporating machine learning methods and automatic energy calibration.

Index Terms —gamma-ray spectroscopy, isotope identification, SNIP  background removal, Gaussian deconvolution, peak detection, AIC/BIC model selection, mixed spectra, Savitzky–Golay filter, Compton continuum

I. I NTRODUCTION Radioactive isotopes emit gamma-ray photons at discrete, isotope-specific energies when their unstable nuclei transition to lower energy states. A gamma-ray spectrometer—typically a high-purity germanium (HPGe) or NaI(Tl) scintillation detector—records these photons as a histogram of counts versus photon energy in keV, commonly called the spectrum . The position of each full-energy peak (photopeak) in the spectrum uniquely fingerprints the emitting isotope; hence, spectroscopy is widely used in nuclear security, environmental monitoring, medical isotope production quality control, and astrophysics [ 1 ], [ 2 ].

In practice, radiation fields are rarely mono-isotopic. En- vironmental samples, spent nuclear fuel, or mixed waste streams contain several isotopes emitting simultaneously. Their photopeaks may overlap when two emission lines are separated by less than the detector’s energy resolution (typically 1–3 keV for HPGe and ∼ 7% at 662 keV for NaI(Tl)) [ 2 ]. Beyond peak overlap, every spectrum is superimposed on a continuous
Compton-scatter background that elevates the baseline and reduces peak-to-background contrast, degrading both detection sensitivity and quantitative accuracy.

Traditional analysis software (e.g., Genie-2000, PeakEasy) relies heavily on manual intervention and fixed energy calibra- tions, making them ill-suited for automated, high-throughput scenarios [ 7 ]. Recent work has explored machine-learning and deep-learning approaches, but purely data-driven methods require large labelled datasets and often lack physical inter- pretability [ 8 ], [ 9 ]. A signal-processing pipeline grounded in physics—Gaussian peak models, information-theoretic model selection, background estimation—provides a robust, inter- pretable, and data-efficient alternative.
This paper makes the following contributions:
• A fully automated, seven-step gamma-ray analysis pipeline implemented in Python using standard scientific libraries ( scipy , numpy , matplotlib ).
• A rigorous evaluation on five-isotope mixed spectra with quantitative precision, recall, and F1 metrics.
• A clear exposition of each algorithmic step with mathemat- ical derivations, facilitating reproducibility and extension.
II. P ROBLEM  S TATEMENT
A. Motivation
Automated isotope identification from mixed spectra is challenging for three principal reasons:

(1) Peak Overlap. When two isotopes emit gamma rays at close energies (e.g., Ba-133 at 356.0  keV and Eu-152 at 344.3  keV , a separation of only ∼ 12  keV ), the detector cannot resolve the two photopeaks; they merge into a single broadened structure. Reporting only the dominant centroid misses one isotope entirely.

(2) Compton Background. Every photon that undergoes incomplete energy deposition within the detector contributes to a continuous Compton-scatter continuum beneath the pho- topeaks. This background, if not properly removed, inflates apparent peak areas and spawns spurious peaks [ 3 ].
(3) Variable Activity and Noise.  Source activity governs the number of counts per channel. Low-activity sources produce noisy spectra where genuine peaks may be buried in statistical
fluctuations, while dominant sources can saturate nearby channels.
B. Objective
The goal of this work is to design and implement an automated pipeline that:

1) Suppresses the Compton background without distorting photopeaks. 2) Reliably detects all photopeaks, including those arising from low-activity isotopes. 3) Identifies and resolves overlapping doublets through model-based deconvolution. 4) Extracts physically meaningful features (centroid, FWHM , area, asymmetry) from each resolved component. 5) Maps extracted components to known isotopes with high precision and recall.
III. D ATA  D ESCRIPTION A. Dataset Overview

The dataset consists of 15 unique simulated mixed gamma- ray spectra stored as plain-text files. Each file contains two columns representing energy (in keV) and corresponding counts, recorded over a measurement time of 600 seconds. In addition, each file includes a header section that provides the activity values of all isotopes present in the spectrum. These activity values are used exclusively as ground-truth labels for evaluation purposes.

A. Classification Metrics

B. Interpretation of Metrics

Precision = 1.000. Every isotope reported by the pipeline as present was genuinely present in the ground-truth label. This perfect precision indicates that the combination of the SNR gate, second-derivative validation, and multi-line confirmation rule eliminates all false positives—no spurious isotopes were identified.
Recall = 0.806.  Approximately 80.6% of all isotopes actually present in the spectra were correctly detected. The remaining ∼ 19.4% are false negatives—missed isotopes. These primarily arise from:
• Low-activity isotopes whose photopeaks are buried in noise and fall below the SNR threshold.
• Severely overlapping doublets where the double-Gaussian fit converges to an incorrect solution (e.g., one component absorbs signal from both true peaks).
• Single-line isotopes (Cs-137) whose only photopeak is obscured by a nearby dominant peak.

F1-Score = 0.892. The harmonic mean of precision and recall reflects strong overall identification performance. The asymmetry between precision (1.0) and recall (0.806) reveals that the pipeline is conservative : it reports confident identifica- tions and avoids guessing, at the cost of occasionally missing weak sources.
C. Strengths and Limitations

The SNIP algorithm effectively removes the Compton contin- uum for all tested spectra, confirmed by visual inspection. The AIC/BIC overlap detection correctly resolved the Ba- 133/Eu-152 doublet near 350  keV in the majority of test cases, recovering both centroids to within ± 5  keV.

The primary limitation is sensitivity to low-count peaks. Because the SNR threshold is derived from the first 200 channels of the spectrum, it may over-estimate the noise floor in spectra with significant low-energy activity, causing borderline peaks to be rejected. Additionally, the pipeline currently assumes a pre-calibrated energy axis; any drift in the calibration would shift peak centroids outside the ± 8  keV matching tolerance, producing false negatives.
VI. V ISUALIZATION  A NALYSIS
The complete visualisation for each spectrum was produced as a multi-panel figure (Fig. VI ):
A. Full-Spectrum View (Top Panel)

The top panel shows the full gamma-ray spectrum plotted on a logarithmic count scale. The measured spectrum is displayed in blue, illustrating the variation of counts with energy across a wide range. Vertical colored lines indicate the reference energies of known isotopes, and the alignment of observed peaks with these reference positions confirms the presence of corresponding isotopes in the spectrum. The logarithmic scale is essential for visualizing the large dynamic range of the data, allowing both high-intensity peaks (such as Cs- 137 at 662 keV and Co-60 peaks at higher energies) and lower-intensity peaks (such as Ba-133 at lower energies) to be observed simultaneously. Additionally, the plot highlights regions where peaks are closely spaced, making overlap visually evident and emphasizing the need for advanced analysis techniques.

VII. F UTURE  W ORK
The current pipeline establishes a robust signal-processing baseline. Six directions for future development are identified:
A. Machine Learning Classification

The feature vectors { f j } (centroid, FWHM , area, asymmetry) extracted per component form a natural input for supervised classifiers. A Random Forest [ 10 ] or a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) operating on localised spectral windows could learn non-linear boundaries in feature space that a simple energy-match threshold cannot capture. This would
be particularly beneficial for discriminating between closely spaced isotopes (e.g., Ba-133 vs. Eu-152) when only partial peak overlap occurs.
B. Activity Estimation

Extending the pipeline from  classification  (presence/absence) to quantification (source activity in Bq) would significantly increase its practical utility. The peak area A j is proportional to activity through:
A src ,k ∝ A j ε ( E j )  I γ ( E j )  T  , (26)

where ε ( E j ) is the detector efficiency, I γ the branching ratio, and T the measurement duration. Incorporating efficiency curves from calibration data would enable quantitative isotope characterisation.
C. SGSD-Based Full-Spectrum Fitting

The Sequential Gamma-ray Spectrum Deconvolution (SGSD) approach [ 11 ] models the entire spectrum as a sum of isotope response functions rather than analysing individual peaks. By sequentially identifying and subtracting isotope contributions from the full spectrum, SGSD handles highly complex, densely packed spectra more robustly than peak-centric methods. Integrating SGSD into the current pipeline would provide a cross-validation mechanism and improve performance at high isotope multiplicities.
D. Data Expansion
The present evaluation uses a limited synthetic dataset. Collecting additional experimental spectra covering:
• More mixture combinations (3-, 4-, and 5-isotope subsets),
• Different activity ratios and absolute activity levels,
• Real-world detector noise and gain instabilities, would allow more rigorous training and evaluation of machine- learning models and test the robustness of the signal-processing steps.
E. Extended Isotope Library

Expanding the reference database beyond the current five isotopes to include additional gamma-emitting radionuclides (e.g., Mn-54, Zn-65, I-131, Tl-208) would broaden the applica- bility of the pipeline to environmental monitoring and nuclear security screening scenarios.
VIII. C ONCLUSION

This paper presented a physics-grounded, seven-step auto- mated pipeline for identifying radioactive isotopes in mixed gamma-ray spectra. The pipeline integrates the SNIP back- ground removal algorithm, Savitzky–Golay–based robust peak detection with SNR gating, AIC/BIC-driven overlap detec- tion, multi-Gaussian deconvolution, and area-weighted isotope matching.
Evaluated on mixed spectra containing five isotopes (Ba-133, Eu-152, Cs-137, Na-22, Co-60) recorded over 600 seconds, the system achieved a precision of 1.000 , recall of 0.806 ,

and an F1-score of 0.892 . The perfect precision confirms zero false positives, validating the conservative identification logic. The recall of 80.6% highlights the main remaining challenge: detection of low-activity isotopes and resolution of severely overlapping doublets.

Future work will address these limitations through supervised machine-learning classifiers on the extracted feature vectors, automatic energy calibration, full-spectrum SGSD fitting, and an expanded experimental dataset. The pipeline as described provides a transparent, reproducible, and extensible foundation for automated gamma-ray spectroscopy.

Their photopeaks may overlap when two emission lines are separated by less than the detector’s energy resolution (typically 1–3 keV for HPGe and ∼ 7% at 662 keV for NaI(Tl)) [ 2 ]. Beyond peak overlap, every spectrum is superimposed on a continuous

Compton-scatter background that elevates the baseline and reduces peak-to-background contrast, degrading both detection sensitivity and quantitative accuracy.

Traditional analysis software (e.g., Genie-2000, PeakEasy) relies heavily on manual intervention and fixed energy calibra- tions, making them ill-suited for automated, high-throughput scenarios [ 7 ]. Recent work has explored machine-learning and deep-learning approaches, but purely data-driven methods require large labelled datasets and often lack physical inter- pretability [ 8 ], [ 9 ]. A signal-processing pipeline grounded in physics—Gaussian peak models, information-theoretic model selection, background estimation—provides a robust, inter- pretable, and data-efficient alternative.

This paper makes the following contributions:

II. P ROBLEM  S TATEMENT

A. Motivation

Automated isotope identification from mixed spectra is challenging for three principal reasons:

(1) Peak Overlap. When two isotopes emit gamma rays at close energies (e.g., Ba-133 at 356.0  keV and Eu-152 at 344.3  keV , a separation of only ∼ 12  keV ), the detector cannot resolve the two photopeaks; they merge into a single broadened structure. Reporting only the dominant centroid misses one isotope entirely.

(2) Compton Background. Every photon that undergoes incomplete energy deposition within the detector contributes to a continuous Compton-scatter continuum beneath the pho- topeaks. This background, if not properly removed, inflates apparent peak areas and spawns spurious peaks [ 3 ].

(3) Variable Activity and Noise.  Source activity governs the number of counts per channel. Low-activity sources produce noisy spectra where genuine peaks may be buried in statistical

fluctuations, while dominant sources can saturate nearby channels.

B. Objective

The goal of this work is to design and implement an automated pipeline that:

1) Suppresses the Compton background without distorting photopeaks. 2) Reliably detects all photopeaks, including those arising from low-activity isotopes. 3) Identifies and resolves overlapping doublets through model-based deconvolution. 4) Extracts physically meaningful features (centroid, FWHM , area, asymmetry) from each resolved component. 5) Maps extracted components to known isotopes with high precision and recall.

A. Classification Metrics

Table III summarises the pipeline’s performance across all test spectra.

B. Interpretation of Metrics

Precision = 1.000. Every isotope reported by the pipeline as present was genuinely present in the ground-truth label. This perfect precision indicates that the combination of the SNR gate, second-derivative validation, and multi-line confirmation rule eliminates all false positives—no spurious isotopes were identified.

Recall = 0.806.  Approximately 80.6% of all isotopes actually present in the spectra were correctly detected. The remaining ∼ 19.4% are false negatives—missed isotopes. These primarily arise from:

• Low-activity isotopes whose photopeaks are buried in noise and fall below the SNR threshold.

• Severely overlapping doublets where the double-Gaussian fit converges to an incorrect solution (e.g., one component absorbs signal from both true peaks).

• Single-line isotopes (Cs-137) whose only photopeak is obscured by a nearby dominant peak.

F1-Score = 0.892. The harmonic mean of precision and recall reflects strong overall identification performance. The asymmetry between precision (1.0) and recall (0.806) reveals that the pipeline is conservative : it reports confident identifica- tions and avoids guessing, at the cost of occasionally missing weak sources.

C. Strengths and Limitations

The SNIP algorithm effectively removes the Compton contin- uum for all tested spectra, confirmed by visual inspection. The AIC/BIC overlap detection correctly resolved the Ba- 133/Eu-152 doublet near 350  keV in the majority of test cases, recovering both centroids to within ± 5  keV.

C. SGSD-Based Full-Spectrum Fitting

The Sequential Gamma-ray Spectrum Deconvolution (SGSD) approach [ 11 ] models the entire spectrum as a sum of isotope response functions rather than analysing individual peaks. By sequentially identifying and subtracting isotope contributions from the full spectrum, SGSD handles highly complex, densely packed spectra more robustly than peak-centric methods. Integrating SGSD into the current pipeline would provide a cross-validation mechanism and improve performance at high isotope multiplicities.

D. Data Expansion

The present evaluation uses a limited synthetic dataset. Collecting additional experimental spectra covering:

• More mixture combinations (3-, 4-, and 5-isotope subsets),

• Different activity ratios and absolute activity levels,

• Real-world detector noise and gain instabilities, would allow more rigorous training and evaluation of machine- learning models and test the robustness of the signal-processing steps.

E. Extended Isotope Library

Expanding the reference database beyond the current five isotopes to include additional gamma-emitting radionuclides (e.g., Mn-54, Zn-65, I-131, Tl-208) would broaden the applica- bility of the pipeline to environmental monitoring and nuclear security screening scenarios.
